lead: An RF amplifier is linear only for small signals. Drive it harder and the output compresses; feed it two close tones and it creates new tones that were never at its input, some of them right inside the wanted band. The 1 dB compression point, the third-order intercept (IIP3) and the spurious-free dynamic range turn 'linear enough' into numbers on a datasheet. Noise sets the weakest signal a receiver can use; these numbers set the strongest signal it can survive beside it.
prereq: You need: dB and dBm, and the receiver noise floor from noise figure and sensitivity.

sections.h3: Gain compression and the 1 dB point

blocks.text: Model a memoryless amplifier as y = a₁x + a₂x² + a₃x³, where x is the input voltage, y the output voltage, a₁ the small-signal gain and a₂, a₃ constants. For an input A cos ωt the output at ω has amplitude a₁A + (3/4)a₃A³. When a₃ is negative (the usual case: the device runs out of voltage or current) the gain a₁ + (3/4)a₃A² falls as A rises. That is gain compression. A positive a₃ would give gain expansion instead. The a₂ term makes second harmonics and a DC shift.

On a dB plot of output power against input power, the small-signal line has slope 1: 1 dB more input gives 1 dB more output. The real curve bends below it. The input 1 dB compression point P1dB,in is the input power at which the measured output is 1 dB below the straight line. The output compression point P1dB,out is the measured output at that input, the number datasheets quote. So

blocks.where: all powers in dBm; G is the small-signal gain in dB. The straight line at P1dB,in reads P1dB,out + 1 dB.

blocks.text: Setting the gain drop to 1 dB in the cubic model gives A²<sub>1dB</sub> = 0.145|a₁/a₃|. A strong off-channel signal near P1dB,in lowers the gain for the weak wanted signal too: blocking, or desensitisation.

sections.h3: Two tones, IM3 and the intercept point

blocks.text: In a two-tone test two equal tones at f₁ and f₂, each of power P<sub>in</sub>, enter the amplifier. The cubic term creates third-order intermodulation (IM3) products at 2f₁ − f₂ and 2f₂ − f₁. With tones at 900.0 and 900.2 MHz the IM3 products land at 899.8 and 900.4 MHz, inside any filter that passes the tones. Their amplitude is (3/4)|a₃|A³, so the IM3 output rises 3 dB for every 1 dB of input, while the wanted output rises 1 dB per dB.

Extend both straight lines: they cross at the third-order intercept point. Its input value is IIP3 and its output value is OIP3 = IIP3 + G. The crossing is extrapolated; the real amplifier compresses well before it. In the cubic model A²<sub>IIP3</sub> = (4/3)|a₁/a₃|, so IIP3 is 10 log₁₀(1.333/0.145) = 9.6 dB above P1dB,in. Real amplifiers are not pure cubics, so measured gaps of 9 to 12 dB are common.

blocks.where: OIM3 is the output power of each IM3 product in dBm; P<sub>out</sub> = P<sub>in</sub> + G is the output per tone in dBm. Input-referred, IM3 = 3P<sub>in</sub> − 2·IIP3.

blocks.text: A measurement gives IIP3 directly. If ΔP is the gap in dB between the output per tone and the output IM3 product, then ΔP = 2(IIP3 − P<sub>in</sub>), so IIP3 = P<sub>in</sub> + ΔP/2. IM3 is often quoted relative to the tone in dBc; −40 dBc is 10 dB cleaner than −30 dBc.

In a chain, input intercepts combine as powers in milliwatts: 1/IIP3 = 1/IIP3₁ + G₁/IIP3₂ + G₁G₂/IIP3₃ + …, with gains as linear ratios. This is the mirror image of Friis: later stages see the signal after gain, so the last stages usually limit linearity, while the first stage limits noise.

The spurious-free dynamic range (SFDR) runs from the input-referred noise floor N up to the per-tone input at which the input-referred IM3 just equals N. Setting 3P<sub>in</sub> − 2·IIP3 = N gives P<sub>in</sub> = (2·IIP3 + N)/3, and SFDR = P<sub>in</sub> − N:

blocks.where: SFDR in dB; IIP3 and N in dBm, both referred to the input; N = −174 + 10 log₁₀B + NF.

blocks.text: At the output, G appears on both sides of 3Pout − 2·OIP3 = N + G and cancels. Blocking dynamic range uses compression instead: BDR = P1dB,in − N. Compression and IM3 also spread a transmitter's energy outside its channel, which is how the same numbers reappear in the spectral mask of transmitter architectures.

examples.question: A two-tone test applies two tones of −10 dBm each to an amplifier. The output shows 10 dBm per tone and IM3 products at −30 dBm. A single-tone sweep gives P1dB,out = 19 dBm. Find G, the IM3 level in dBc, IIP3, OIP3, P1dB,in, and how far the tones sit below compression.
steps: Gap between tone and IM3 at the output: ΔP = 10 − (−30) = 40 dB, so IM3 = −40 dBc.
IIP3 = P<sub>in</sub> + ΔP/2 = −10 + 20 = 10 dBm; OIP3 = IIP3 + G = 30 dBm.
Check with the output form: OIM3 = 3P<sub>out</sub> − 2·OIP3 = 3 × 10 − 2 × 30 = −30 dBm, as measured.
P1dB,in = P1dB,out + 1 − G = 19 + 1 − 20 = 0 dBm; the straight line there reads 20 dBm, 1 dB above the measured 19 dBm.
The tones sit 10 dB below P1dB,in, and IIP3 is 10 dB above P1dB,in, close to the 9.6 dB of a pure cubic.
examples.answer: G = 20 dB, IM3 = −40 dBc, IIP3 = 10 dBm, OIP3 = 30 dBm, P1dB,in = 0 dBm, and the tones are backed off 10 dB from compression.

examples.question: A two-tone test on the LNA–mixer–IF chain of the noise figure chapter (G₁ = 15 dB, G₂ = 10 dB) gives these stage intercepts: LNA IIP3 = −5 dBm, mixer IIP3 = +5 dBm, IF amplifier IIP3 = +10 dBm. Find the cascaded IIP3 and the SFDR in the 10 MHz channel, where the chain's input noise floor is −100.8 dBm. Which stage limits linearity?
steps: Convert to milliwatts: IIP3₁ = 0.316 mW, IIP3₂ = 3.16 mW, IIP3₃ = 10 mW; G₁ = 31.62, G₁G₂ = 316.2.
The IF amplifier's term (31.6) is 71 % of the sum: the last stage limits linearity, while the LNA limited the noise. With only the LNA and mixer, IIP3 would be 1/13.16 mW = −11.2 dBm.
Top of the range: P<sub>in</sub> = (2(−16.5) + (−100.8))/3 = −44.6 dBm per tone. Check: IM3 = 3(−44.6) − 2(−16.5) = −100.8 dBm, equal to the floor.
examples.answer: Cascaded IIP3 = −16.5 dBm, SFDR = 56.2 dB; the IF amplifier sets the linearity, so less gain before it (or a more linear IF stage) is the fix.

traps: Treating IIP3 as a safe input. It is an extrapolated point about 10 dB above P1dB,in; an amplifier driven there is deep in compression.
Mixing input and output intercepts: OIP3 = IIP3 + G. Using OIP3 in the input form 3P<sub>in</sub> − 2·IIP3 shifts the IM3 answer by 2G.
Writing P1dB,out = P1dB,in + G. The measured output at compression is 1 dB below that: P1dB,out = P1dB,in + G − 1.
Combining intercepts like Friis with the first stage dominant. For IIP3 the later stages are multiplied by the gain ahead of them, so they dominate.
Using an output noise floor with IIP3 in the SFDR formula. Both must be referred to the same point.

quiz.a: P1dB,in is the input power at which the measured output is 1 dB below the small-signal straight line. IIP3 is the input power at which the extrapolated fundamental and IM3 lines (slopes 1 and 3) meet.

quiz.q: Why does IM3 rise 3 dB per dB of input while the wanted tone rises 1 dB per dB?
quiz.a: The IM3 product comes from the a₃x³ term, so its amplitude is proportional to A³; in dB that multiplies every input change by 3. The wanted output is proportional to A.

quiz.q: An amplifier has G = 15 dB and IIP3 = 5 dBm. Two tones are each −20 dBm. Find the output per tone and the IM3 output.
quiz.a: P<sub>out</sub> = −5 dBm. OIP3 = 20 dBm. OIM3 = 3(−5) − 2(20) = −55 dBm, that is −50 dBc.

quiz.q: A receiver has input noise floor −100 dBm and IIP3 = −5 dBm. Find SFDR, and the SFDR if the noise floor rises by 6 dB.
quiz.a: SFDR = (2/3)(95) = 63.3 dB. With N = −94 dBm, SFDR = (2/3)(89) = 59.3 dB, 4.0 dB less: SFDR moves by two-thirds of any change in N or IIP3.

quiz.q: A two-tone test at −25 dBm per tone gives a 50 dB gap between the output tone and the IM3 product. Find IIP3.
Why is SFDR smaller than P1dB,in − N?
quiz.a: IM3 grows three times faster than the tones and reaches the noise floor long before compression. With P1dB,in about 9.6 dB below IIP3, P1dB,in − N exceeds (2/3)(IIP3 − N) whenever IIP3 − N is more than about 29 dB, which is true of every practical receiver.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wideband amplifiers show memory effects, where distortion depends on past signal values; they are modelled with Volterra series and memory polynomials rather than one a₃. The second-order intercept (IIP2) matters in direct-conversion receivers, where second-order products fall at DC. Search for 'IIP2 direct conversion' and 'memory polynomial model'.

figure.caption: The worked example's amplifier (G = 20 dB). At −10 dBm per tone the wanted output is 10 dBm and IM3 is −30 dBm, 40 dB lower; the slope-1 and slope-3 lines meet at IIP3 = 10 dBm, OIP3 = 30 dBm, far above the 1 dB compression point at 0 dBm in, 19 dBm out.

spec.aria: Output power against input power per tone. The wanted output follows a slope-one line and bends over towards saturation near 21 dBm, crossing 19 dBm at 0 dBm input, the 1 dB compression point. The IM3 output follows a slope-three line. At minus 10 dBm input the wanted output is 10 dBm and IM3 is minus 30 dBm, a gap of 40 dB. Extended dashed lines meet at 10 dBm input and 30 dBm output, the intercept point.
